sections.heading: Two woods, built to the same standard.
sections.body: We can build a fence for your location from either pine or cedar, and in varying heights. Pine is the budget-conscious choice for a long run of privacy fencing; cedar costs more and holds up better to weather and insects over time. Which one makes sense usually comes down to the length of the run and how long you want to leave it alone.

sections.heading: Privacy, security and shade.
sections.body: Custom pine and cedar privacy fencing built for security, shade, and a clean finished look. Height and picket spacing change what the fence actually does — a full-privacy panel and a spaced picket run are different fences for different problems, and it is worth deciding which one you are buying before the posts go in.

sections.heading: The posts decide how long it lasts.
sections.body: Pickets and rails are the part you see, but they are not the part that fails first. A wood fence usually goes because the posts rotted at the ground line or worked loose in soft soil, and once that starts the rest follows regardless of how good the boards were. Depth, spacing and how the post is set are what buy the years. This is also why a fence that looks fine from the road can still be near the end of its life — push on it, and if the posts move, the fence is telling you something the pickets are hiding. It is worth knowing before you spend money on replacement boards that will outlive what holds them up.

sections.heading: Pick the height for the job, not the look.
sections.body: Height is the decision people most often get wrong, partly because it is hard to picture from a catalogue. Six feet is the usual privacy answer because it breaks sightlines from a neighbouring yard at standing height. Four feet contains pets and marks a front boundary without walling the property off, which is often what a front yard actually wants. Eight feet screens completely where local rules allow it. It is worth knowing that height drives cost more than the extra material suggests, because taller fencing needs deeper posts and more bracing to stay upright in wind. A four-foot fence bought for privacy is money spent on the wrong problem, and it cannot be raised later without starting again.

faqs.q: How tall should a privacy fence be?
faqs.a: Six feet is the usual answer for privacy, because it screens sightlines from a neighbouring yard at standing height. Four feet contains pets and marks a front boundary without closing the property off. Eight feet screens completely where that is permitted locally. Height also changes the price more than most people expect, since it changes post depth as well as material.

faqs.q: Does a wood fence need sealing?
faqs.a: It extends the life, particularly on pine. Cedar tolerates being left alone better than pine does, which is part of what the extra cost buys. Either way the posts fail before the pickets do, so how they were set matters more to the lifespan than what gets put on the surface afterwards.

sections.heading: The practical choice for a long run.
sections.body: Durable, budget-conscious fencing for homes, pets, businesses, and larger properties. Chain-link covers more ground per dollar than any other fence we build, which is why it tends to win on acreage, on commercial yards, and anywhere the job is containment rather than privacy.

sections.heading: Sports and court enclosures.
sections.body: The same system goes up tall — we have built chain-link at tennis courts, where the fence is doing a different job again: keeping a ball in rather than keeping anything out. Taller runs need heavier posts and closer spacing, so it is worth saying up front what the enclosure is for.

sections.heading: Two numbers change the price.
sections.body: Chain-link is priced by height and by the gauge of the wire, and the right answer depends on what the fence is doing. A dog run and a commercial yard are different fences even though both are chain-link, so it is worth saying which you need before comparing quotes.

sections.heading: Cost per foot is the whole argument.
sections.body: Chain-link covers more ground per dollar than any other fence we build, which is why it keeps winning on long runs, acreage and commercial yards where the job is containment rather than privacy. It also takes weather without needing to be sealed or painted, and a damaged section can be replaced without touching the rest of the run. What it does not do is screen anything, which is the trade you are making. Slats can be woven through the mesh where some privacy is wanted without the cost of a wood run, though they are a compromise rather than a substitute. If the fence exists to keep something in or out over distance, this is usually the right answer.

faqs.q: What height of chain-link do I need?
faqs.a: Four feet contains most dogs and marks a boundary. Six feet is the common choice for security and for keeping larger animals in. Taller runs are used for courts and sports enclosures, where the job is keeping a ball in rather than keeping anything out — those need heavier posts and closer spacing.

sections.heading: Two rails or three.
sections.body: Rail count is the main decision on split rail. Two rails suit a boundary or a decorative run; three hold larger animals more reliably. It changes both the price and what the fence can actually do, so it is worth settling early.

sections.heading: Corners do the work.
sections.body: On a long pasture run the straight sections are the easy part. Corners and gate posts take the strain of every rail pulling against them, so they are set deeper and braced harder than the rest — and it is where a cheap job shows itself first, usually within a season.

sections.heading: Rail count is the real decision.
sections.body: Split rail is chosen for two quite different reasons and the rail count follows from which one applies. As a boundary or a decorative edge along a drive or a property line, two rails do the job and keep the look open — the fence marks without enclosing. As containment for larger animals, three rails hold more reliably, because an animal that can get its head through a gap will usually try. Posts and bracing change with it, since a fence that is leaned on carries load the decorative version never sees. Split rail also suits uneven ground better than panel fencing, which is part of why it keeps appearing on acreage where a rigid run would leave gaps at every dip.

sections.heading: Monroe is several fence jobs, not one.
sections.body: The Garden District is the older residential core people mean by that name: the blocks around Forsythe Park and Forsythe Avenue, toward Riverside Drive, with houses that went up in the early twentieth century. Lots are often tighter than a new subdivision. Drives are narrow, and a gate has to clear a car that already sits close to the street. A privacy fence there is usually a side yard and a back yard, not a field. Tell us if a rear garage or a shared drive is in the way, because that changes where the gate can go.

sections.heading: The east bank is a short run, and a different one.
sections.body: Downtown Monroe is on the east bank of the Ouachita. A job there is often short: a gate, a repair, or a run along a small commercial yard rather than a new backyard enclosure. The truck has to approach on the street that actually reaches the fence. A one-way block and a tight alley are worth saying on the call. The riverfront itself is not where most residential fences are. The houses just back from it are. If the line is near the water, say so. A slope toward the bank is a layout problem, not a detail to discover after the posts are on the trailer.

sections.heading: The bayou and the campus are not the same call.
sections.body: Bayou DeSiard runs through the city, and the University of Louisiana Monroe campus sits along it. Houses on the bayou and rentals near the campus get mixed up on the phone because both are 'by the bayou.' They are different. A rental usually wants a plain privacy or chain-link run that a tenant can live with, and the person who can approve the fence may not be the person who answers the door. A bayou lot may slope toward the water, and the line is rarely a clean rectangle. Standing water after a rain is common on the low side. We need to know which of those we are walking before we talk about material.

sections.heading: North Monroe and the south side are opposite drives.
sections.body: North Monroe runs up from the older core toward Black Bayou Lake. US 165 is the road people use when they are heading that way, on toward Sterlington. Yards there are often deeper than a Garden District lot, and a side fence can be a long run. The south side, including the area people call Booker T. Washington, is its own set of streets. A lot of those calls are repairs and replacements of fences that have already had a hard life, not a first fence on a bare new lot. 'South Monroe' is too big to dispatch from. The cross street is the useful part. A fence off one south-side road and a fence off another are not the same trip once the truck is across the river.

sections.heading: We are in West Monroe. Monroe is across the river.
sections.body: The shop is 205 Mane St, Ste C, West Monroe, LA 71292. Monroe is the other side of the Ouachita. Interstate 20 crosses the river, and the downtown bridges do too. That crossing is ordinary. It is not a reason to treat a Monroe address as out of range, and it is also not zero. A fence just across the bridge is a short addition to a West Monroe day. A fence on the far south side, or well up US 165, is a longer drive. We would rather say that than imply a crew parked in every neighborhood. If you are choosing a company by time, ask on the call what the run looks like. A page cannot know which direction the truck is already heading.

sections.heading: Clay that stays wet, and a spring storm.
sections.body: Monroe sits on ground that holds water. A low spot along the bayou, or a yard that stands wet after a rain, is a different post than the same fence on a high, drained lot. We set posts for the ground we are actually in. A length and a height on the phone are a start, not a finished price. Spring storms are the other local fact. Wind takes the section next to a post that was already soft, and a solid privacy fence catches more of that wind than an open chain-link run. After a storm, photograph the fence before anything is hauled off. Repair versus replacement is usually obvious from the posts, and a picture of those posts saves a wasted trip.

faqs.a: Yes. The city requires a fence permit before a fence is built or rebuilt. Front-yard height and side-yard height are not the same rule, and guessing them is how a finished fence has to move. The guide on this site cites the ordinance and the planning office. Read that before posts go in.

sections.heading: Containment and boundary are different jobs.
sections.body: A fence keeping cattle in and a fence marking a property line are built differently. Livestock decides height, spacing and how solid the corners have to be, because the animals lean on it; a boundary run can be lighter. Saying which one you need is the single most useful thing on a first call.

sections.heading: Long runs change the economics.
sections.body: On acreage the cost is in linear feet, so the choice of material matters more than it does on a back garden. Split rail suits pasture and grazing; chain-link covers ground cheaply where containment matters more than looks. We build both, and on a long run it is worth walking the line before deciding.

sections.heading: North Louisiana ground is not flat and not dry.
sections.body: Slope, soft ground and standing water all change how posts have to be set. A fence line that crosses a low spot or a drainage cut needs planning rather than improvising on the day, which is why we would rather look at it than quote it blind.

sections.heading: Animals lean on fences.
sections.body: A boundary fence marks a line; a containment fence resists an animal pushing against it, and the two are built differently even when they look similar from the road. Posts are set deeper and closer, corners and gate posts are braced because that is where the load concentrates, and the rail count is chosen for what is being held rather than for appearance. Two rails suit a boundary or a decorative run. Three hold larger animals more reliably. Pasture also tends to mean longer runs over uneven ground, which changes how the line is laid out — following the contour rather than cutting across it keeps the fence tight and keeps gaps from opening at the low points where an animal will find them.

pages.seoDescription: Commercial fencing in Monroe, West Monroe and Ouachita Parish — business premises, yards, storage and larger properties.

sections.heading: Security first, appearance second.
sections.body: Chain-link is durable, budget-conscious fencing for homes, pets, businesses, and larger properties, and on commercial work it usually wins for the same reason it wins on acreage: it covers the most ground per dollar and it does not hide what is behind it. Where appearance matters at the frontage, ornamental and metal fencing adds security without closing the property off visually.

sections.heading: The gate is the part that gets used.
sections.body: On a commercial site the fence is mostly static and the gate works every day, which means the gate is where wear, cost and frustration concentrate. Width has to suit the largest vehicle that will ever need in, including deliveries rather than just staff vehicles. Hardware takes far more cycles than a residential gate ever will. Where the opening sits relative to the approach matters too: a gate that requires a vehicle to stop on a road to line up will get treated roughly, whichever way it swings. Getting the width and the approach right at the start costs very little; correcting either one afterwards means moving posts.

sections.heading: The yard usually has to keep working.
sections.body: Most commercial fencing goes up around a site that cannot close for the week. Sequencing the work so access stays open is a scheduling question more than a fencing one, and it is easier to solve before we start than halfway through.

sections.heading: Why commercial runs usually end up chain-link.
sections.body: Commercial fencing is normally bought by the foot rather than by the panel, and that changes which material makes sense. Chain-link covers distance more economically than anything else, takes weather without being sealed or painted, and can have a damaged section replaced without disturbing the rest of the run — which matters when the fence surrounds something that has to keep operating. It also makes the yard visible, which is a security advantage as often as it is a drawback. Where appearance matters at a street frontage, the usual answer is to treat that stretch differently rather than to pay for the whole perimeter twice. Height is a separate decision from material and worth settling on its own terms.

sections.heading: A gate is a lever on a post.
sections.body: Every gate is a weight hanging off one side of a post, and the wider the gate the harder it pulls. Most sagging gates are not bad gates — they are gates hung on a post that was set for fence and not for leverage. A gate post wants to be bigger, deeper and better braced than the run it sits in.

sections.heading: Width is the decision that costs money later.
sections.body: A drive gate that is narrow enough to be awkward gets clipped, and a gate that has been clipped never hangs right again. Measure for the vehicle that actually uses it, including the trailer, before settling on a width.

sections.heading: The gate should look like part of the run.
sections.body: We fit gates to wood, chain-link and ornamental fencing so the gate reads as part of the fence rather than as something bolted on afterwards.

sections.heading: Measure for the trailer, not the car.
sections.body: The most common regret on a drive gate is width, and it is the one thing that cannot be adjusted afterwards without moving a post. People measure for the vehicle they drive every day and then discover the gate is tight for a trailer, a mower, a delivery truck or a contractor who needs to get a machine into the back yard. A gate that is slightly too narrow gets clipped, and a gate that has been clipped never hangs true again. Walk it through in your head with the widest thing that will ever need to pass, then add room for the fact that nobody lines up perfectly on a first attempt. Extra width costs very little at the start.

faqs.q: Why do gates sag?
faqs.a: Almost always because the gate post was set for fence rather than for leverage. A gate is a weight hanging off one side of a post, and the wider the gate the harder it pulls. A gate post wants to be bigger, deeper and better braced than the run it sits in — which is cheap to do at the start and expensive to correct afterwards.

sections.heading: The posts usually decide it.
sections.body: Panels and pickets are cheap to replace; posts are not. If the posts are still solid, a repair is nearly always the better buy. When the posts have gone — leaning, rotted at ground level, or pulling out — you are rebuilding the fence around bad foundations, and that is the point at which replacement stops being the expensive option.

sections.heading: Taking it out is part of the job.
sections.body: Removal and haul-off is the part people forget when comparing a replacement to a new build. It is real work — old posts set in concrete do not come out easily — and it belongs in the quote rather than appearing as a surprise.

sections.heading: Worth changing what did not work.
sections.body: A replacement is the one chance to change height, material or layout without paying twice. If the old fence was the wrong height, or the gate was in the wrong place, say so before we start rather than rebuilding the same problem.

sections.heading: How to tell which one you need.
sections.body: The test is the posts. Individual broken pickets, a sagging gate or a couple of damaged panels are repairs, and repairs are worth doing when the structure underneath is sound. Once posts are rotted, leaning or moving when pushed, the arithmetic changes: replacing posts means pulling the fence apart anyway, and a patchwork of new posts under old boards tends to mean returning to the same fence again in a year or two. The other honest signal is how many repairs you have already paid for. A fence that has been fixed three times is usually telling you what it needs. Walking the line and pushing on posts every few feet will answer this faster than any estimate.

sections.heading: Wind finds the weak post.
sections.body: A storm rarely takes a whole fence evenly. It finds the post that was already marginal and takes the sections either side of it, which is why a repair that only replaces the panels tends to fail again in the next blow. We repair leaning posts, damaged panels, broken gates and storm-related fence damage.

sections.heading: A fallen limb is a different job.
sections.body: A tree or a large limb across a fence usually destroys the posts as well as the panels, and sometimes moves the fence line. That is closer to a rebuild of the affected run than a repair, and it is worth knowing which one you are looking at before making a claim.

sections.heading: Send a picture before we drive out.
sections.body: A photograph of the damage from a few feet back tells us more than a description does, and it usually decides whether the job is a repair or a replacement without anyone making a trip.

sections.heading: Photograph it first.
sections.body: North Louisiana weather takes fences down, and the instinct after a storm is to clear the mess. Take photographs before you do. Whether an insurer covers the damage is between you and your policy, but the claim is far easier to make when there is a record of what the fence looked like before anything was tidied, from a few angles, with something in frame for scale. It also helps to note which way things fell, because wind direction and a fallen limb tell a different story from a post that had already rotted. None of that can be reconstructed once the debris is gone. If a fence is down across a boundary or blocking access, secure the gap first and photograph what you moved.

faqs.q: Will my insurance cover a storm-damaged fence?
faqs.a: That is between you and your insurer and depends on your policy, so it is worth asking them before committing to work. What helps either way is photographs of the damage taken before anything is moved or cleared.

sections.body: Calhoun is an unincorporated community in western Ouachita Parish. Interstate 20 has exits for it, including US 80 and LA 151, and US 80 itself runs through the crossroads. From 205 Mane St in West Monroe, the drive is west on that corridor. You do not cross the Ouachita to get there the way a Monroe job does. It is still a real drive, past the edge of West Monroe, and a five-acre line is not the same trip as a backyard inside the city. Say whether the gate is on US 80, on a parish road off it, or down a drive that a truck has to commit to. Those are different arrivals.

sections.heading: Pasture and a house lot are different fences.
sections.body: Most of what people call a Calhoun fence is longer than a city backyard. A line around a house, to keep a dog in and a road out, can be wood, vinyl, or chain-link. A line across pasture is usually split rail or a farm fence, and the rail count follows the animal. Two rails mark a boundary. Three hold larger animals more reliably, because an animal that can get its head through will try. Corners and gate posts carry the load when something leans. On a long run the material decides the job more than it does on a short city fence, which is why we would rather walk the line than price it from a pin on a map. The materials calculator will count posts for a length you already know. It will not know the dips.

sections.heading: Open ground, wet spots, and a line that is not straight.
sections.body: Western Ouachita ground is not a flat subdivision pad. A fence that crosses a low spot or a drainage cut has to be planned, or it opens a gap at the bottom where the land dips. Posts in soil that stays wet after a rain do not get the same hole as posts on a firm rise. Calhoun lots often include both in one run: a dry stretch along the road and a soft stretch farther back. Tell us about creek crossings, a pond, and any place the line has to stop for a gate wide enough for a tractor or a trailer. Width is cheap to add before the posts are set and expensive after.

sections.heading: The front of the property is still a residential fence.
sections.body: Acreage does not mean the whole job is farm fence. The stretch people see from US 80 or from the parish road is often the part that should look like a house: privacy on the sides of a patio, a gate at the drive, and something lower or more open where the view is the point. Mixing materials on one property is normal. The mistake is building the pasture fence up to the porch, or building a short privacy fence and discovering the animals are not held by it. Say what each stretch is for. If a neighbor's fence already stands on one side, we need to know whether we are tying to it or leaving it alone.

sections.heading: Calhoun is not inside Monroe or West Monroe.
sections.body: Calhoun is outside those city limits, in Ouachita Parish. Monroe's permit rules do not travel with you just because the mailing address feels close to the twin cities. The parish guide on this site is the one written for unincorporated Ouachita, including the ditch rule along a public road. Confirm it with the Ouachita Parish permit office before posts go in. A city-limit line is not always obvious from the driveway, and a fence across a roadside ditch is a problem the parish already wrote down. We will not guess which side of a boundary you are on.

pages.pointsHeading: Longer lines than a city lot.

points.description: Field and boundary runs where the length, not the panel, is the job. Corners and braces matter because animals lean.

points.description: Containment over a longer house lot or a yard where you need to see through the fence.

points.title: Wood or vinyl at the house
points.description: Privacy around a patio or a pool of space behind the house, even when the rest of the property is open.

faqs.q: Is Calhoun close enough to be worth a small job?
faqs.a: The shop is in West Monroe, and Calhoun is west on US 80 and I-20, so it is one of the closer rural drives. A short repair and a half-mile of pasture are still different trips. Ask on the call if you are comparing companies by who is actually nearby that day.

faqs.q: Whose permit rules apply in Calhoun?
faqs.a: Calhoun is unincorporated Ouachita Parish, not the City of Monroe and not West Monroe. Use the parish guide, then confirm with the Ouachita Parish permit office. Do not apply the Monroe height rules to a Calhoun line.

pages.heading: Fencing in Sterlington, LA.
pages.intro: Privacy fencing and house lots in Sterlington, north of Monroe on US 165, with the Ouachita River and Bayou DeSiard in the same part of the parish. We drive it from West Monroe. There is not a Sterlington yard.
pages.seoTitle: Fencing Sterlington LA | Twin City Fence
pages.seoDescription: Privacy fencing and fence repair in Sterlington, Louisiana, north on US 165. Newer subdivisions and older houses, from a West Monroe shop.

sections.heading: North on US 165, not a hop across the river.
sections.body: Sterlington sits north of Monroe on US 165, between the twin cities and Bastrop. The highway follows the Ouachita and Bayou DeSiard country on the way up. From 205 Mane St in West Monroe we cross into Monroe and keep going north. That is a longer drive than a fence in the Garden District and a shorter one than Bastrop or Ruston. It is still the same crew and the same phone. If the house is on a new street off the highway, the name of that street matters more than 'Sterlington.' A subdivision entrance off US 165 and a house on an older road toward the river are different last miles.

sections.heading: Privacy fencing is the usual ask.
sections.body: A lot of Sterlington work is a house on a newer street where the lot is big enough for a real backyard and the neighbor is close enough that privacy is the point. Wood and vinyl are the two versions of that fence. Wood is pine or cedar. Vinyl is the one you are not painting. Both are solid, so both catch wind, and a six-foot panel in an open subdivision is a sail in a spring storm. Gate posts have to be heavier than line posts because the gate is a lever. Measure the drive for the widest thing that will use it, including a trailer, before the opening is set. A gate that is a foot too narrow gets clipped, and a clipped gate never hangs right again.

sections.heading: Not every Sterlington fence is a new subdivision.
sections.body: The town is older than the newest streets. Houses on the roads that were there first often need a repair, a partial replacement, or a fence that has to meet an existing line instead of starting from a bare lot. Posts that have stood in ground that stays wet are the usual failure. If the posts are solid, replacing pickets or a panel is the smaller job. If the posts move when you push them, you are looking at a rebuild of that run. A photo of the worst post and of the whole line from a few steps back is enough for us to tell those apart on a lot of calls. Say if a tree or a ditch is in the line. Both change the layout.

sections.heading: Water nearby changes the ground, not the brochure.
sections.body: Sterlington's setting is the river and the bayou, which is a reason yards hold water and a reason some lots are not rectangles. It is not a reason to claim every house is waterfront. If your line runs toward the Ouachita or toward Bayou DeSiard, say that. A slope, a flood-prone corner, and a drainage ditch the fence must not block are things we need before posts are spaced. We do not publish a soil type or a flood map on this page. We look at the yard. The same honesty applies to the drive: north Ouachita is in range, and it is not the same trip as a West Monroe backyard.

sections.heading: Sterlington is a town. Monroe's permit page is not its code.
sections.body: Sterlington has its own limits. We have not written a Sterlington permit page, and we will not pretend Monroe's height rules or the parish guide automatically cover a lot inside the town. Ask the Town of Sterlington what it requires before you build. If the property is outside the town, in unincorporated Ouachita, the parish guide is the page we do have, and the parish office is who confirms it. An HOA, if the street has one, can add height and material rules on top of whatever the town requires. We do not keep those private rules. You will know them better than we will. Mention them when you call.

points.title: Wood privacy
points.description: The usual new backyard fence on a Sterlington street. Pine for the longer budget-minded run, cedar when weather is the reason you are paying more.

points.title: Vinyl privacy
points.description: The same enclosure without a paint cycle. Posts and gates are still the structural part.

points.title: Repair
points.description: A leaning run, a storm section, or a gate that dropped. Often the right job on an older lot.

points.title: Chain-link
points.description: When the need is a dog or a back line you can see through, not a solid wall.

faqs.q: Do you actually come to Sterlington, or is this a page for show?
faqs.a: We come. The shop is in West Monroe, and Sterlington is north on US 165 past Monroe. It is a scheduled drive, not a truck sitting at the highway. Ask what the timing looks like if that is how you are choosing.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit in Sterlington?
faqs.a: Ask the Town of Sterlington. We do not publish the town's fence rules here because we have not verified them line by line. If the lot is outside the town, in the parish, start with the Ouachita Parish guide and confirm it with the parish office.

pages.ctaCopy: Call the number on this page with the street, the length you think you need, and whether the posts that are there now are solid.

pages.heading: Fencing in Ruston, LA.
pages.intro: Residential fencing and rental properties in Ruston, in Lincoln Parish, about 30 miles west of Monroe on I-20. Louisiana Tech is the landmark. The shop is still in West Monroe, so a Ruston job is a planned trip, not a same-block call.
pages.seoTitle: Fencing Ruston LA | Twin City Fence
pages.seoDescription: Residential and rental fencing in Ruston, Louisiana, about 30 miles west on I-20 near Louisiana Tech. Permit rules are the City of Ruston's. We are based in West Monroe.

sections.heading: A half hour west, and we will not pretend otherwise.
sections.body: Ruston is the seat of Lincoln Parish. Interstate 20 is the drive from the twin cities, past Calhoun, about 30 miles. From 205 Mane St in West Monroe that is a real trip in the same direction as Calhoun and then farther. We take the work. We do not describe it as local in the way a West Monroe backyard is local. If you need someone who can look at a gate this afternoon, say that on the call and we will tell you whether we are the right truck. A planned fence, a rental turn, or a line you already know the length of is the kind of Ruston job that fits a shop in Ouachita Parish.

sections.heading: Rentals near the campus are a specific kind of fence.
sections.body: Louisiana Tech University is in Ruston, and a share of the housing around it is rentals. Those fences get leaned on, and the person paying for the fence is often not the person living there. A straightforward wood or chain-link run, with a gate that survives being used every day, is the usual request. Fancy layout is rarely the point. Durability and a clean line the next tenant does not have to interpret are. Tell us if the property is a rental, who will meet the crew, and whether a previous fence is coming out. Removal of old posts set in concrete is part of the work, and it belongs in the conversation at the start. Houses that are not rentals, farther from campus, are a different call: privacy for a yard, a gate sized for the vehicle that actually uses the drive.

sections.heading: Ruston is more than the blocks by the university.
sections.body: The older streets and the edges of town have the same mix we see in any small city. A repair where posts have rotted at the ground. A privacy fence on a new backyard. Chain-link where the job is containment. Vinyl where nobody wants to paint. We build those. What we will not do is invent a Ruston price from a Monroe average. The drive is part of the job, the lot is part of the job, and a slope or a tree in the line is part of the job. Photos of the line, the worst post, and the drive entrance are enough to decide whether we should come look or whether you are better with someone already in Lincoln Parish that week.

sections.heading: Ruston has its own rules. Ask the city.
sections.body: Ruston is not Ouachita Parish and it is not Monroe. The permit pages on this site for Monroe, West Monroe, and the unincorporated parish do not govern a lot inside the City of Ruston. Check with the City of Ruston before posts go in. We are not stating a height, a setback, or a fee on this page, because we have not verified Ruston's current fence rules and we will not copy an old number. If the property is outside the city, in Lincoln Parish, ask the parish. An HOA rule, if one applies, is on top of that and is yours to know. Bring it up. A fence built to the wrong height is the expensive kind of mistake.

sections.heading: The call is more useful if the line is already paced.
sections.body: Pace the run or step it off. Note corners and every gate, with the width you need. Say wood, vinyl, or chain-link, and whether dogs, privacy, or a rental turnover is the reason. If a tree, a ditch, or a slope breaks the line, say where. Then call. The materials calculator on this site will turn a length into a count of posts and pickets so you can see the scale. It does not price the drive to Ruston and it does not know the city's rules. Use it to understand the pile of material. Use the call to find out whether we should be the ones who put it in.

faqs.q: Is Ruston too far?
faqs.a: It is far enough to say so. About 30 miles west on I-20, in Lincoln Parish, past Calhoun. We will take a planned job. We will also tell you on the phone if the timing does not make sense compared with someone already there.

faqs.q: Do Monroe's fence rules apply in Ruston?
faqs.a: No. Check with the City of Ruston. This site's Monroe, West Monroe, and Ouachita Parish permit guides are for those places only. We are not publishing Ruston height limits or fees here.

pages.ctaCopy: Call the number on this page with the address, the approximate length, and whether anyone has to approve the work besides you.

pages.heading: Fencing in Swartz, LA.
pages.intro: House lots and acreage in Swartz, just northeast of Monroe along US 80 and LA 139. Close to the twin cities, outside the Monroe city rules, and still dispatched from the West Monroe shop.
pages.seoTitle: Fencing Swartz LA | Twin City Fence
pages.seoDescription: Residential and acreage fencing in Swartz, Louisiana, northeast of Monroe on US 80 and LA 139. Unincorporated Ouachita Parish. Based in West Monroe.

sections.heading: Northeast of Monroe, on LA 139 off US 80.
sections.body: LA 139 leaves US 80 on the east side of Monroe and runs northeast through Swartz as the houses thin out toward open parish. It is the Old Bastrop Road side of the metro, along the country east of Bayou DeSiard, not the US 165 side that goes through Sterlington. From 205 Mane St in West Monroe we cross the Ouachita and come out this way. It is one of the shorter drives outside the two cities. It is still a parish road at the end, not a city block. The landmark that helps is the highway: US 80 if you are on the south edge, LA 139 if you are up in Swartz proper. A driveway number and a cross street beat a neighborhood nickname.

sections.heading: Residential fences, with room that Monroe lots often lack.
sections.body: A Swartz house lot is often larger than a lot in the Garden District, which changes the fence. There is usually a real backyard, a longer side line, and a drive that has to fit a truck. Privacy fencing in wood or vinyl is the common request when the neighbor is near and the road is not. Chain-link shows up when the point is a dog or a back line you want to see through. Gates are the part that fails first if the post was set like a line post. Tell us the width you need, including a trailer or a mower, and whether the gate is for people, vehicles, or both. A walk gate and a drive gate are different posts.

sections.heading: Some of these properties stop being backyards.
sections.body: Farther up LA 139 the lots open into acreage. That is split rail, farm fence, or a mix: privacy at the house and an open fence on the field. The purpose of each stretch has to be named. A decorative rail will not hold what a containment fence holds, and a solid privacy fence across a pasture is a lot of sail in a storm for no gain. Ground that holds water shows up here the same way it does closer to the bayou. A low spot needs a plan so the fence does not gap at the bottom. If the line crosses a ditch beside a parish road, stop and read the parish rule before anyone sets a post in it. That one is already written down, and it is easier to respect than to undo.

sections.heading: Older fences out here usually fail at the post.
sections.body: Swartz has houses that have had the same fence for a long time. The panels can look fine while the post at ground level is gone. Push on a few posts. If they move, replacing the boards is a temporary kindness. Storms do the same sort of editing: they take the weak section and leave the rest. Photograph the damage before it is cleared if you might need a record of it. We repair leaning posts, broken gates, and runs that need a partial rebuild. If the whole line is tired, replacement includes pulling the old posts, which is real work when they were set in concrete. That belongs in the scope, not as a surprise.

sections.heading: Swartz follows the parish, not the City of Monroe.
sections.body: Swartz is in Ouachita Parish, outside the City of Monroe. Do not use the Monroe permit page for a Swartz yard. The parish guide on this site is written for unincorporated Ouachita. It is the right starting point, and the parish permit office is who confirms it, especially if you are near a city limit and are not sure which side the lot is on. We will not guess. Height limits that are not published in a way we can cite are left to that office. If a subdivision off LA 139 has its own rules, those are private. Bring them to the call so we do not build a fence the neighborhood will reject.

faqs.q: Is Swartz the same trip as Monroe?
faqs.a: It is the same direction once we have crossed the river, and then northeast on US 80 and LA 139 instead of into downtown or the Garden District. Close, and still its own drive. The shop is in West Monroe.

faqs.q: Do I need a Monroe permit in Swartz?
faqs.a: No. Swartz is outside the city. Start with the Ouachita Parish guide and confirm with the parish permit office. Monroe's front-yard heights do not apply just because Swartz is nearby.

pages.ctaCopy: Call the number on this page. Say house yard or acreage, and name the road. LA 139 and US 80 are different arrivals.

pages.heading: Fencing in Bastrop, LA.
pages.intro: Residential and small-town fencing in Bastrop, the Morehouse Parish seat, about 25 miles north of Monroe on US 165. A different parish from the shop in West Monroe, and a drive we will describe as a drive.
pages.seoTitle: Fencing Bastrop LA | Twin City Fence
pages.seoDescription: Fence installation and repair in Bastrop, Louisiana, about 25 miles north on US 165 in Morehouse Parish. Based in West Monroe. Check the City of Bastrop for permits.

sections.heading: US 165 north, about 25 miles.
sections.body: Bastrop is north of Sterlington on US 165, in Morehouse Parish. From the shop at 205 Mane St in West Monroe the route is through Monroe and up that highway, on the order of 25 miles. People also come in on LA 139, which ends at the courthouse square downtown. Either way it is not a West Monroe errand. We schedule Bastrop. We do not imply a crew lives there. If the fence is a single gate you need looked at today, ask whether the timing works. If it is a yard you are planning, the miles are just part of arranging the day, the same as any job outside the parish we start in.

sections.heading: Most Bastrop fences are houses, not fields.
sections.body: In town the work looks like other small-city fencing. Wood or vinyl privacy on a backyard. Chain-link where you need containment and you want to see through. A gate that has sagged because the post was never set for the weight. Ornamental metal on a front where a solid wall would hide the house. Older blocks near the courthouse square have tighter approaches, the same problem as any downtown: the truck needs a way in, and a gate on a narrow side yard has to be measured, not guessed. Newer edges of town have deeper lots and longer side lines. Say which one you are, and whether the old fence is still standing. Hauling it off is part of a replacement.

sections.heading: Morehouse Parish opens up past the houses.
sections.body: Beyond the city limits the properties get larger. Pasture and boundary fencing show up, and the question is what the fence has to hold. Split rail and farm fence are the tools for that. A house yard at the front of the same property may still want privacy. Build them as two decisions. Ground in this part of north Louisiana holds water in the low places, and a line that crosses a ditch or a soft corner needs that called out before the spacing is set. We are not claiming a soil survey. We are saying we want to see the low spot rather than hear 'it's pretty flat' and find standing water on the day.

sections.heading: The same spring weather, a longer drive after it.
sections.body: Spring storms do not stop at the Ouachita Parish line. A privacy fence is still a sail, and wind still finds the soft post. After a storm in Bastrop, the useful thing is a photo of the posts and of the whole run before the debris is stacked. That tells us whether you are looking at a repair of a section or a rebuild. It also matters if you are talking to an insurer, which is between you and the policy, not something we decide. Because the drive is longer, a clear photo saves a trip that was only going to confirm what the picture already showed. If the fence is down across a road or a neighbor's drive, make the gap safe first and photograph what you moved.

sections.heading: Bastrop's rules are Bastrop's. We will not borrow Monroe's.
sections.body: Morehouse Parish is outside every permit guide this site currently publishes. Monroe, West Monroe, and unincorporated Ouachita do not apply to a lot in Bastrop. Check with the City of Bastrop if you are inside the city, and with Morehouse Parish if you are outside it. We are not stating heights, fees, or setbacks here. Those numbers go stale, and an invented one is worse than a gap. If an HOA or a landlord has a material or height rule, that is yours to bring. We will build to a rule you can show us. We will not guess one from a neighboring city.

faqs.q: How far is Bastrop from you?
faqs.a: About 25 miles north of Monroe on US 165, and farther than that from the shop in West Monroe. Sterlington is on the way. It is a scheduled trip. Ask on the call if you need to know whether we can be there when you need us.

faqs.q: Which permit office do I call?
faqs.a: The City of Bastrop if the property is in the city. Morehouse Parish if it is outside the city limits. Do not use the Monroe or Ouachita Parish guides for a Bastrop address. We have not published Bastrop's fence heights or fees.

pages.heading: Fencing in Farmerville, LA.
pages.intro: Lake lots and pasture fencing in Farmerville, in Union Parish, near Lake D'Arbonne. About 30 miles from Monroe, and a longer trip from the shop in West Monroe than a fence in Ouachita Parish.
pages.seoTitle: Fencing Farmerville LA | Twin City Fence
pages.seoDescription: Lake-property and pasture fencing in Farmerville, Louisiana, near Lake D'Arbonne in Union Parish. Based in West Monroe. Confirm permits with the town or the parish.

sections.heading: Union Parish is a planned trip.
sections.body: Farmerville is the seat of Union Parish, northeast of the twin cities, about 30 miles from Monroe and farther from 205 Mane St in West Monroe. Lake D'Arbonne is the reason a lot of people know the name. We will drive it for a job that is ready to be built or walked. We will not describe Farmerville as if it were a neighborhood of West Monroe. The honest version is the same one we use for Ruston and Bastrop: say what the fence is, send a photo of the line if you have one, and ask whether the day works. If someone already based in Union Parish can start sooner, you should know that before you wait on us.

sections.heading: A lake lot is not a rectangle in a subdivision.
sections.body: Property on Lake D'Arbonne often has a slope toward the water, a line that follows the shore instead of a survey square, and a view somebody does not want a solid wall across. That pushes the fence choice. Privacy may belong on the side yards, between houses, and not across the bank. An open fence, ornamental or split rail, keeps the lake visible where that is the point. Access is the other half. Camp roads and shared drives are narrow, and a trailer of posts has to be able to turn around. Tell us about the approach before we arrive with the wrong truck. If the lot floods or the bank moves, say that too. We are not publishing a lake rule or a building line. The town or the parish has that, and the plat has the corners.

sections.heading: Away from the water, the fence is for animals or for a boundary.
sections.body: Union Parish past the lake roads is pasture and timber-edge property. A fence that keeps animals in is built differently from a fence that only marks a line. Posts are closer and deeper, corners are braced, and the rail count matches what is being held. Two rails suit a boundary or a look. Three hold larger animals more reliably. A long run across uneven ground should follow the contour so gaps do not open at the low points, which is where an animal will test the fence. Mix this with a house yard if you need both, and do not use one material for both jobs unless it actually does both. Walking that line matters more here than it does on a flat city lot, because the dips are the bid.

sections.heading: Farmerville itself is a small-town fence.
sections.body: Inside town the calls are familiar. A backyard privacy fence. A repair where the bottom of the post has gone. A gate that sags. Chain-link for a dog. The streets are not a metro grid, so the approach and a place to park the truck are worth a sentence on the phone. Older fences in town have often been patched. If you have paid to fix the same run more than once, the posts are telling you something. Replacement includes taking the old fence out. That is heavier work than it looks when the posts are concreted in. Put it in the scope at the start.

sections.heading: Ask Farmerville or Union Parish. Our other guides do not cover this.
sections.body: Nothing on this website about Monroe, West Monroe, or Ouachita Parish permits applies in Farmerville. If the property is in town, check with the Town of Farmerville. If it is in the parish outside town, check with Union Parish. Lake-edge rules and ordinary backyard rules may not be the same, and we have not verified either one well enough to quote them. We will not put a height or a fee on this page. An HOA or a lake association rule, if your road has one, is private and is your document to share. Build to the rule you can show. Guessing from a neighboring parish is how fences get taken down.

faqs.q: Do you fence lake property and pasture, or only houses?
faqs.a: Both, and they should be talked about as different fences. A lake lot often wants privacy on the sides and an open line toward the water. Pasture wants a fence that holds animals. A town backyard is the ordinary privacy or repair job. Say which one is yours.

faqs.q: Where do I ask about a permit?
faqs.a: The Town of Farmerville if you are in town, and Union Parish if you are outside it. This site does not have a Farmerville permit guide. The Monroe and Ouachita pages do not apply here, including on the lake.

sections.heading: Push on the posts before you buy boards.
sections.body: Pickets and panels are the part you see. Posts are the part that fails. If the posts are still tight in the ground, replacing a few boards, a rail, or a latch is usually the right spend. If the posts move when you push them, or they are soft at the soil line, new boards are going onto a fence that is already done. Ouachita Parish ground holds water. A post that has been sitting in a wet line along the Ouachita, or in a low backyard in West Monroe, often rots at the surface while the pickets still look fine. That is the check we make before recommending a repair.

sections.heading: Gates, panels, and sections, not just storm piles.
sections.body: Storm damage has its own page because a tree on a fence is a different job. Everyday repair is quieter: a gate that sags because the post was set for fence and not for the leverage of the gate, a section a vehicle clipped, a dog that found the one loose board, a chain-link run that is leaning after years of people climbing it. Wood, chain-link, and ornamental fences all come in. Vinyl repairs depend on whether the broken piece is a rail or a post and whether that style is still made. Bring a photo. It often tells us whether to bring boards or to come and look at posts.

sections.heading: Wet soil is why the same repair fails twice.
sections.body: A post reset in the same soft hole, without thinking about water, leans again. Monroe and West Monroe yards after a heavy rain show you where the water sits. A repair on that line either moves the post, sets it so water is not the whole story, or it is a temporary fix and we should say so. Slope changes it too. A fence that stair-steps down toward a drainage ditch needs the low end planned, not improvised. If the line is the property line and you are not sure where that is, sort that out before posts are pulled. Moving a repaired fence is the expensive version of a survey.

sections.heading: Length, material, and whether the posts move.
sections.body: On the call, three things matter: about how many feet are damaged, what the fence is made of, and whether the posts are solid. A phone photo of the worst post and of the whole run from a few steps back is enough for a lot of small repairs. A whole side of a yard wants a visit. We are at 205 Mane St, Ste C, West Monroe. Most repair work is in West Monroe, Monroe, and the rest of Ouachita Parish. If you are comparing a repair to a new fence, the materials calculator and the permit guides are the next stop after this page, especially if the repair is about to become a replacement tall enough that the city cares.

faqs.q: Is a repair worth it?
faqs.a: Usually yes when the posts are solid and the damage is a section, a gate, or some pickets. When the posts are rotted or loose, you are paying to decorate a fence that needs to be rebuilt. We would rather say that on site than sell boards.

faqs.q: Do you repair chain-link and metal fences too?
faqs.a: Yes. Chain-link that is leaning, ornamental fences with a broken picket or a dragging gate, and wood. Vinyl depends on the parts. A photo is the quickest way to know.

faqs.q: How is this different from storm repair?
faqs.a: Storm work is a fence that weather or a tree took down, often with an insurance photo to take first. This page is the ordinary repair: age, a vehicle, a gate, a few bad posts. If a storm did it, use the storm damage page so you photograph it before anything is cleared.

sections.heading: Privacy without a paint can.
sections.body: A vinyl privacy fence does the same job as a wood privacy fence: it breaks the sightline into the next yard. Picket and spaced styles mark a front yard without walling it off. Homeowners in Monroe and West Monroe usually ask about vinyl after they have painted a pine fence once and do not want to do it again. That is a fair reason. Vinyl does not need stain. It also does not hide a bad post. The panels are only as straight as what holds them, and a vinyl fence with a leaning post looks worse than a wood one because the panels stay bright while the line goes crooked.

sections.heading: North Louisiana sun is not a mild test.
sections.body: Summer here is long. Dark vinyl runs hotter and shows heat distortion sooner than a light color, which is why white and clay are the styles you see holding up on streets in West Monroe. We will talk about color on site rather than sell a dark fence that looks sharp in a photo and waves by August. Rails and pickets also expand. A fence built tight on a cold morning can bind a gate in July if the hardware and the gaps were not planned for it. That is a build detail, not a reason to avoid vinyl. It is a reason to build it with the season in mind.

sections.heading: Usually near pine on a short run, not a bargain on a long one.
sections.body: We do not print a dollar-per-foot price. Length, height, gates, and the ground move it too much, and a number given without walking the line gets revised. In relative terms, vinyl privacy often lands near a pine privacy fence and sometimes above it once the gates and the style are counted. Cedar costs more than pine and still wants occasional care. Vinyl is the one you are buying so you can leave the surface alone. Chain-link is cheaper per foot when the job is keeping a dog in a long yard and privacy does not matter. If privacy is the point, vinyl and wood are the conversation, and the permit rules for height are the same either way.

sections.heading: The expensive parts are the ones you do not see.
sections.body: Vinyl posts on a privacy fence need to be set for wind. A six-foot solid panel is a sail in a spring storm coming across open yards in Ouachita Parish. Gate posts need to be heavier than line posts, same as wood, because the gate is a lever. A drive gate that is too narrow gets clipped, and vinyl does not forgive a clip the way a board you can replace does. Measure for the widest thing that will use the drive, including a trailer. We install from our West Monroe shop at 205 Mane St, Ste C, across Monroe and West Monroe. If the fence is new rather than a repair, check the Monroe or West Monroe permit guide before the posts go in. Height and the front-yard rules are local, and they are easier to read first than to rebuild.

faqs.q: Is vinyl cheaper than wood?
faqs.a: Sometimes it is close to pine privacy, and sometimes the style and the gates put it higher. It is not the cheap fence. Chain-link is, when you do not need privacy. Call with the length and the style and we will look at the line before naming a figure.

faqs.q: Does vinyl work in Louisiana heat?
faqs.a: Light colors do better than dark ones. The build has to leave room for the material to move, and the posts have to be set for wind on a solid panel. Those are the details that decide whether it still looks right in a few summers.

faqs.q: Can you match an existing vinyl fence?
faqs.a: Sometimes, if that profile is still sold. A photo of the post, the rail, and the panel from the side tells us whether a repair section will match or whether the run wants to be replaced together.

sections.heading: Security and a boundary, not privacy.
sections.body: An aluminum picket fence lets you see through it. That is the point on a front yard in Monroe, on a commercial frontage where you want the building visible, and anywhere a solid wall would look like the back of the property facing the street. It will not stop a sightline. If that is what you need, the privacy fence page is the wood or vinyl conversation. Ornamental fence marks the line, keeps a casual cut-through honest, and holds a gate. It is a poor choice for a dog that can squeeze pickets, unless the spacing is chosen for that animal and not for the look.

sections.heading: The old iron fences around town explain the choice.
sections.body: There is plenty of older steel and iron fence in Monroe and West Monroe, and a lot of it is being painted because it rusts at the joints. Aluminum ornamental fence is what people switch to so the maintenance is hardware and posts, not a wire brush. It is lighter, which is nice to carry and which means the post has to be set properly or the whole run feels flimsy in a wind. We do not describe it as wrought iron. If you have true iron you want repaired, say that, because repair and a new aluminum run are different work.

sections.heading: The gate is where ornamental fence gets expensive.
sections.body: A walk gate is straightforward if the post is big enough and deep enough. A drive gate is the piece that sags, drags, and gets hit. Width is the decision you cannot undo without moving a post. Measure the vehicle and the trailer, then add room for a bad angle on the way in. On a corner lot, the gate and the fence also have to stay out of the sightline at the intersection. West Monroe and Monroe both treat corner lots differently from a mid-block backyard. The permit guides spell out whose rules apply. Read them before we set a corner post you then have to move.

sections.heading: Front yards, small commercial lots, and pool surrounds.
sections.body: The usual residential job is a front or side yard that a privacy fence would close off, especially on streets where the house is the thing you want to see. Small commercial lots on the West Monroe side use it along the street and chain-link or a taller fence at the back. Pool surrounds are a different rule set: a fence around a pool has to do a safety job, and the city's pool-barrier rules are not the same as a decorative front fence. We will not guess those on a sales page. If the fence is for a pool, say so on the call and check the permit guide for the city you are actually in. We work from 205 Mane St, Ste C, West Monroe, on both sides of the river.

faqs.q: Is aluminum the same as wrought iron?
faqs.a: No. Aluminum ornamental fence is the lower-maintenance stand-in for that look. Existing iron can sometimes be repaired. A new run is usually aluminum, and we will say which one you are buying.

faqs.q: Will it give me privacy?
faqs.a: No. You can see through it. That is why people put it on a front yard. For privacy, look at wood or vinyl.

faqs.q: Can it go around a pool?
faqs.a: Only if it meets the barrier rules for that city, which cover height, gaps, and the gate latch. Tell us it is a pool fence at the start, and check the Monroe or West Monroe permit page before anyone digs.

sections.heading: Six feet is the usual answer, and it is not always allowed.
sections.body: A six-foot solid fence blocks the sightline from a neighboring yard at standing height. Four feet does not, no matter how nice the pickets are. Eight feet screens more and needs a stronger build, and it is the height most likely to run into a local limit. Monroe, West Monroe, and the unincorporated parish do not share one rule. A backyard in the city and a lot outside the city limits can be different jobs. The permit guides on this site point at the city's own text for height, front yards, and corner lots. Read the one that matches the address before you fall in love with a picture of an eight-foot fence.

sections.heading: Same job, different upkeep.
sections.body: Pine is the common privacy fence because it covers the run for less than cedar or a fancy vinyl style. It wants seal if you care how it looks in five years, and the posts still outlast the argument about stain. Cedar costs more and weathers better. Vinyl privacy is the option when you do not want to coat it at all. All three fail the same way if the posts are shallow in wet Ouachita ground: the panels stay pretty and the line leans. A privacy fence is a sail. Spring wind across an open yard in West Monroe will find the weak post. That is why post depth and spacing are the part of the quote worth understanding, not just the price of the board.

sections.heading: The pretty side and the property line are separate questions.
sections.body: People ask which side of the fence the 'good side' faces. That is a build choice and a neighbor choice, and it is cheaper to agree before posts are in the ground. Where the fence sits is not a choice we get to invent. If you are not sure the line is where the old fence was, a survey is less painful than moving a finished run. Shared fences and fences just inside your line get handled differently, and an HOA can be stricter than the city about height, color, and which side faces out. If you have an HOA, their paper rules over a page like this one.

sections.body: Twin City Fence is at 205 Mane St, Ste C, West Monroe. Privacy fences are most of the residential work in Monroe and West Monroe: back yards in neighborhoods off the river, side yards where a patio faces a neighbor, and the occasional full enclose. Chain-link with slats is a compromise when budget is the whole story and full privacy is not. It is not the same fence. If you want a number, we need the approximate length, the height you are allowed to build, and whether a gate has to fit a mower or a truck. The materials calculator will count boards and posts for a length you already know. It will not know your property line or your city's height cap. Those are the permit pages.

faqs.q: How tall should a privacy fence be?
faqs.a: Six feet is the height that actually blocks a standing neighbor. Taller than that depends on the city and, if you have one, the HOA. Four feet will disappoint you if privacy was the reason you called.

faqs.q: Wood or vinyl for privacy?
faqs.a: Wood if you want the lower material cost of pine or the longer-weathering cedar and you will live with some upkeep. Vinyl if you want to stop painting. The posts matter more than that choice. Both need to be set for wet ground and wind.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit?
faqs.a: Often the answer depends on height, the front yard, and whether you are in Monroe, West Monroe, or the parish. Use the permit guide for the place the property actually sits, and call the office if the guide and your lot do not obviously match.

sections.heading: Why this page does not list a price per foot.
sections.body: Twin City Fence does not publish a rate card. A 100-foot pine privacy fence on flat, open ground and a 100-foot fence that steps down a wet slope with two gates and a stump in the line are different jobs, and a single number would be a fiction. Anyone who gives you a firm figure from a phone description, without seeing the line, is guessing. We would rather walk it. What this page can do is put the choices in order so you know what you are comparing when two estimates do not match.

sections.heading: What usually costs more than what.
sections.body: Chain-link usually costs less per foot than the other fences we build. It wins on long runs, dogs, and commercial yards where privacy is not the job. Pine privacy costs more than chain-link and is the usual backyard fence. Vinyl privacy often lands near pine and sometimes above it once style and gates are included. Cedar costs more than pine. Aluminum ornamental is usually the highest per foot of the residential fences we install, because the posts and the gates are a large share of a shorter, more detailed run. Those are relative statements, not a price list. They are also typical of how bids come out in Monroe and West Monroe, not a promise that your yard will sort itself the same way if the ground is difficult.

sections.kicker: The things that move a bid
sections.heading: Length is obvious. The rest surprises people.
sections.body: Height costs more than the extra board suggests, because taller fence needs deeper posts and more brace in the wind. Gates cost more than the same width of fence, and a drive gate costs more than a walk gate. Removing an old fence, especially posts set in concrete, is part of a replacement and it gets forgotten when someone prices 'just the new fence.' Trees, a slope toward a ditch, and soil that stays wet along the Ouachita all add work. So does a corner lot, where the fence may have to sit back so drivers can see. None of that shows up in a national average you found online. If a planning table appears under this page later, it will be labeled as an estimate. Until then, the honest figure is the one from a visit.

sections.kicker: How to get a useful number
sections.heading: Measure roughly, then have us look.
sections.body: Pace the run or step it off. Note the corners and every gate, with the width you actually need. Say what the fence is for: privacy, a dog, cattle, a pool, a shop front. Photos of the line, the worst slope, and any old posts help. Then call or use the form. We are at 205 Mane St, Ste C, West Monroe, and we work in Monroe, West Monroe, and Ouachita Parish. The materials calculator will turn a length into a count of posts and pickets so you can see the scale. It does not price labor or haul-off. The permit guides tell you whether height or the front yard is going to change the design before you pay for the wrong fence. Use both. Then get a number from someone who has stood on the line.

faqs.a: Usually the posts, the gates, or whether removal is included. A low bid that skips haul-off or uses fewer posts is not the same fence. Ask each bidder what is in the number.

faqs.q: What decides the price of a fence?
faqs.a: Three things, in this order: the type of fence, how long the run is, and what the ground is doing. Slope, trees, soft ground and existing posts all change the work involved, which is why a figure given over the phone without seeing the line tends to move once someone walks it.

faqs.q: Do you repair fences, or only build new ones?
faqs.a: Both. Leaning posts, damaged panels, broken gates and storm damage are all repair work. Whether a repair is worth doing usually comes down to the posts — panels and pickets are cheap to replace, posts are not.

faqs.q: Should I choose wood or chain-link?
faqs.a: Wood if you want privacy or the look; chain-link if the job is containment over a longer run. Chain-link covers more ground per dollar than anything else we build, which is why it tends to win on acreage and commercial yards. They are different fences for different problems rather than better and worse.

faqs.q: Pine or cedar?
faqs.a: Pine is the budget-conscious choice for a long run of privacy fencing. Cedar costs more and holds up better to weather and insects over time. Which one makes sense usually comes down to the length of the run and how long you want to leave it alone.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a fence?
faqs.a: It depends on where the property sits and what you are building, and rules differ between Monroe, West Monroe and the unincorporated parish. Check with your local permitting office before work starts — and if there is an HOA, check with them too, since they often set height and material rules the parish does not.

faqs.q: How close to the property line can I build?
faqs.a: That is set locally rather than by us, and it is worth confirming before posts go in — moving a finished fence is far more expensive than checking first. If you are unsure where the line actually runs, a survey settles it and prevents the argument that a misplaced fence otherwise starts.

faqs.q: Do you build fences for livestock?
faqs.a: Yes. Split rail suits pasture and grazing, and the rail count is the main decision: two rails suit a boundary or a decorative run, three hold larger animals more reliably. Containment fencing is built differently from a boundary run because animals lean on it.

faqs.q: Do you fit gates as well?
faqs.a: Yes, to wood, chain-link and ornamental fencing. The thing worth settling early is width — a drive gate narrow enough to be awkward gets clipped, and a gate that has been clipped never hangs right again. Measure for the vehicle that actually uses it, including the trailer.

faqs.q: What areas do you cover?
faqs.a: We are based in West Monroe and install across West Monroe, Monroe and the surrounding Ouachita Parish area, travelling further into North Louisiana for larger jobs. If you are not sure whether you are in range, it is worth asking rather than assuming.
